checkpoints: The manifest read — GET /api/files/:fileId — returns file-level facts (fileId, name, mimeType, totalSize, chunkCount), backed by a normalized file(1)→chunk(N) schema rather than embedding an array of chunks in one JSON column.
The chunk-list read — GET /api/files/:fileId/chunks — returns that file's chunks ordered by ascending chunkIndex, each carrying chunkIndex, sha256, size, storageObjectKey.
This normalization keeps the dedup question ('does a chunk with this sha256 already exist') a cheap indexed lookup instead of scanning and parsing a blob.
It also keeps the resumable question ('which chunkIndex is missing') a scan over a queryable ordered set instead of reading the whole array just to infer a gap.
An unknown fileId must return 404 on both routes — never a silently-empty manifest {chunks: []} — because that would be indistinguishable from a file that genuinely exists but is empty.

A real zero-byte upload is the opposite case: a valid, addressable row with chunkCount: 0 and an empty chunks array, so the contract must let a client tell 404 (doesn't exist) apart from 200-plus-empty (exists and is empty).

chunkIndex is what lets the client walk the chunk list in order to reassemble the original file, so a unique constraint on (fileId, chunkIndex) is needed so two chunk rows can never silently occupy the same slot and corrupt reassembly.

The write side must insert the file row and every one of its chunk rows in one transaction, otherwise a crash mid-insert could commit a file row claiming chunkCount: 5 while only 3 chunk rows actually persisted — a manifest that looks valid but can never be reassembled.
Within the TTL window the edge keeps serving the OLD bytes after the origin content changed — the entry doesn't self-correct, it just self-expires once the TTL runs out.
Since ETag is the SHA256 of the bytes, the cached entry also carries the now-WRONG ETag validator for the whole remaining TTL window.
Short TTL + revalidation via If-None-Match is the simplest direction: it shrinks the stale window but is never truly immediate, since you must still wait out the TTL before revalidating.

Explicit purge is immediate in intent, but its hard part is propagating the purge command correctly and completely to every edge replica holding that entry — miss one replica and it keeps serving stale bytes.

Content-addressed URLs put the hash in the path (e.g. /chunk/<sha256>): when bytes change, the hash changes, so the request points at a brand-new cache key — an ordinary MISS — while the old entry has no one calling it, ages out, and gets evicted without any active purge command.

Content-addressed/immutable URLs are the most natural fit here since chunks are already SHA256-addressed — it turns invalidation into a cache-key-selection problem instead of a command-propagation problem; explicit purge is still needed for mutable paths that don't carry a hash.
Because the origin is fully shielded behind the edge — the client has no other way to reach it — the edge tier becomes the only door, and a single edge instance is a single point of failure.

The fix is multiple edge replicas behind a load balancer with health checks, each keeping its own (or a shared tier-2) cache, so a dying edge is simply pulled from rotation instead of taking the whole system down.
The server recomputes each chunk's SHA256 server-side, never trusting a client-supplied hash, and looks that hash up in the chunk_dedup index.
Chunk 1 (AAAA) and chunk 2 (BBBB) hash to values not yet present in the index, so both are a MISS.
MISS handling: the server stores the chunk once under a content-derived storageObjectKey (objects/<sha256[:2]>/<sha256>), inserts a row with ref_count = 1, and writes the full chunk bytes.
Chunk 3 (AAAA again) hashes to the exact same SHA256 as chunk 1, which the index already has a row for, so it is a HIT.
HIT handling: the server writes zero new bytes, reuses chunk 1's exact storageObjectKey, and just bumps its ref_count to 2.
Savings math: totalReferences = 3 chunks uploaded, uniqueChunks = 2 distinct objects stored, so savingsPercent = (3 − 2) / 3 × 100 = 33.33%.

This works without ever comparing files pairwise because the object key is derived from the content hash itself — identical bytes always produce the identical key, unlike naming by userId/filename, where ten identical ISO uploads would become ten unrelated objects.
ref_count makes reuse safe: the object can only be deleted once ref_count drops back to zero, never while any upload still references it.
The server treats the upload as a progress cursor rather than one indivisible operation: it keeps a committed offset per session and advances it by the chunk size each time a chunk is accepted.
On reconnect, the client GETs the session to read the current committed offset, then resumes sending from exactly that byte instead of re-uploading from the start.
The server accepts an incoming chunk only if its claimed offset equals the pending offset it is waiting for.

A mismatch — a stale retry, a duplicated chunk, or two chunks racing — returns HTTP 400 with expectedOffset, refusing to splice bytes into the file at the wrong position instead of blindly appending whatever arrives next.
State is split across two tiers: the live offset lives in Redis for a fast per-PATCH check, while Postgres holds the durable session as the source of truth for recovery.
If Redis loses the key (restart or eviction), the system reconstructs the offset from Postgres and reseeds Redis, rather than wrongly assuming the offset reset to 0.
The cache key is both a correctness decision and an efficiency decision, not just a technical detail.
Keying on $request_uri collapses all reads of the same fileId/chunkIndex onto one cache entry, which is exactly why the hit rate is high.
Query strings or Vary headers should only be folded into the key when they genuinely change the response body.
Adding them when they don't change the body splits one logical resource into many near-duplicate entries, each cold and needing its own MISS, which tanks the hit rate.
TTL is the freshness dial: a longer TTL means fewer trips to the origin but staler data being served.
A shorter TTL plus If-None-Match revalidation stays fresher, at the cost of cheap 304 round-trips to the origin.
Because these chunks are content-addressed (the ETag is the chunk's own SHA256), content that never changes can safely be cached long or treated as immutable.
The overall framing is to pick the key and TTL to maximize hits and protect the origin, subject to never returning a stale or wrong response.
Fixed-size chunking's boundaries are purely positional — a constant 1MB offset from the start of the file — with no regard for content.
Inserting one byte at the very front shifts every downstream 1MB window by one byte, cascading the shift through the rest of the file.

Because SHA256 is deterministic and only identical bytes yield an identical digest, almost every chunk after the insertion point now holds different bytes than yesterday and so hashes differently too.
The dedup index, keyed on that hash, finds no match for nearly the entire new chunk set even though 99% of the file's real content is unchanged — this is fixed-size chunking's boundary sensitivity.
This isn't a reason to abandon fixed-size chunking outright: it stays simple, deterministic, and good enough for fresh, one-shot uploads that are never re-edited.
The point to graduate to content-defined chunking is when the workload is backup or sync — the same file edited repeatedly over time — because only then does the extra cost pay for itself.

Content-defined chunking places boundaries wherever a rolling hash of the content matches a pattern, so an edit only disturbs the handful of chunks around the change while the rest keep their old hashes and still dedup — an edit-resilient model.
The trade-off: chunks become variable-sized instead of a fixed 1MB, and the boundary-detection logic (rolling hash over a sliding window) is meaningfully more complex than simply counting an offset.

Deleting an object the instant one upload is cancelled is wrong because content-defined dedup has already made many logical uploads point at one single physical object, so acting on one upload's say-so can destroy data another upload still shares.
The ref_count mechanism increments each time a chunk HITs — its SHA256 matches an existing object.
The ref_count mechanism decrements each time a reference is removed, such as a session being cancelled or a cleanup job running.
A garbage-collection process runs periodically, scans for objects with ref_count = 0, and deletes exactly those, since reaching zero means no upload references the object anymore.
One failure mode is never deleting (or never running GC): storage leaks without bound because unused objects occupy space forever.
The opposite failure mode is deleting based only on 'this upload was cancelled' without checking ref_count, which destroys another upload's data that still shares that exact object.

A session abandoned midway bumped ref_count for chunks it sent but never calls the reference-removal path because it never explicitly completes or cancels, so those references are held forever without cleanup.

The fix is a session TTL (e.g., the session's Redis key expires after 86400 seconds), plus a job that periodically scans expired sessions and decrements ref_count for every object each expired session referenced.

A PATCH writeChunk handler that takes a client-supplied `sha256` field and uses it directly as the chunk's identity — for both the dedup lookup and the derived storage object key — is trusting client-declared metadata as if it were a cryptographic fact, without ever recomputing the hash from the actual received bytes.

Content-addressable storage systems rely on the invariant that a key always equals the hash of the bytes it points to; skipping the recompute step and substituting a client-asserted value breaks that invariant at the exact point where untrusted input crosses into the storage layer.

If the claimed hash happens to collide with an existing `chunk_dedup` entry, the request is treated as a dedup HIT and returns the object key for that entry — silently serving back bytes that belong to different content than what the client actually uploaded.

If the claimed hash does not yet exist, the handler inserts a brand-new `chunk_dedup` row keyed by that unverified hash, creating an entry whose stored bytes no longer equal the hash of its own key — this is index poisoning, and every future lookup of that hash inherits the corruption.

Because the server never independently verifies the claim, the same bug also lets ordinary transit corruption go undetected: bytes that got mangled in flight are still filed under whatever hash the client originally declared, with no check that the two still agree.

The correct fix is to decode the request bytes first and then compute the SHA256 digest server-side from those exact bytes (e.g. `createHash("sha256").update(data).digest("hex")`), using only that recomputed digest — never the client-supplied value — as the identity for both the dedup lookup and `objectKeyFor(...)`.

The client's `claimedSha` should be downgraded from an identity input to a verification assertion: compare it against the server-recomputed hash, and reject the request with a 400 `sha256_mismatch` error before any lookup or write happens if the two disagree.

This is a general trust-boundary principle, not a hashing-specific one: any identity, key, or address that a client can freely name for data it also supplies must be independently derived or verified server-side, exactly the same discipline applied to validating any other untrusted input.

`Buffer.alloc(CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES)` allocates a full 1MB buffer that Node zero-fills by default, and `Buffer.prototype.copy` only writes as many bytes as actually exist in the given source range — for every full chunk that source range holds a full 1MB, but for the file's final chunk the range runs past `payload.length`, so `copy` writes fewer real bytes and the remainder of the buffer stays at its original zero-fill.

Hashing `buf` instead of the real byte range means the digest for the final chunk is `sha256(real tail bytes + zero padding)`, not `sha256(real tail bytes)` — the padding silently becomes part of what gets content-addressed.

This breaks dedup identity: the same real tail bytes, stored elsewhere as their own complete object or as the true final chunk of another identical file, hash to the digest of just those bytes — a different, unpadded digest — so a lookup against this chunk's padded hash never matches.

It also breaks integrity verification: a check that reads back the actually-stored bytes and re-hashes them (correctly, unpadded) can never reproduce the recorded padded digest, so a file that is not actually corrupt gets flagged as corrupt.

`size: CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES` is hard-coded on every chunk regardless of how many bytes were really copied, so for any file whose length is not an exact multiple of the chunk size, `sum(chunk.size)` comes out larger than the file's true `totalSize` — the invariant that chunk sizes must sum to the file's total size is silently violated alongside the hash bug.
The fix keeps the fixed 1MB windowing scheme untouched and only removes the padding: hashing and sizing must operate on the real byte slice, not an allocated fixed-size window.

Using `payload.subarray(i * CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES, (i + 1) * CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES)` directly avoids the bug entirely, because `subarray` clamps its end to `payload.length` automatically — the final window comes back shorter with no manual `Buffer.alloc` or `copy` step, and hashing that slice plus recording `size: slice.length` makes the last chunk legitimately smaller than 1MB.

With the fix, chunks `0` through `N-2` are computed exactly as before (unaffected, since their source ranges were always full), while the last chunk's hash now represents only real bytes and `sum(chunk.size) === totalSize` holds again, restoring both dedup identity and the size invariant.

Storing the chunk manifest as a single JSONB array on the file row makes sha256 unindexable, since it lives inside array elements rather than as a real column — a global dedup lookup ("does this sha256 exist anywhere?") degrades into scanning and parsing every file's array instead of hitting an index.

The same structural limitation blocks the resumable-upload query "which chunkIndex is missing for this file?" — that answer can only be computed client-side after fetching and parsing the whole array, not expressed as a WHERE clause.

Updating a single chunk under this design requires reading the entire chunks array, mapping over every element to change one, and writing the whole array back in one UPDATE — an N-chunk file rewrites all N chunk entries to change just one, which is significant write amplification.

This read-mutate-write pattern is not concurrency-safe: two requests updating two different chunks of the same file each read the array before either writes back, so whichever update lands second silently overwrites the first request's change — a lost update with no error raised.

Keeping chunkCount as its own hand-maintained column alongside the chunks array creates a second fact about the same data with no single source of truth; nothing stops it from drifting away from the actual chunks.length if a future write path forgets to keep both in sync.

The fix is the normalized file (1) -> chunk (N) model: a ChunkEntity with a unique index on (fileId, chunkIndex) and an index on sha256, with chunkCount derived from COUNT(*) (or trusted only because the insert is transactional) rather than hand-carried.

A JSONB blob is genuinely simpler when the only operation is fetching the whole manifest and handing it to the client in one row read with no join — the trade-off only tips toward normalization once "does this chunk exist" or "which chunk is missing" become the steady-state queries.

The recommendation can be validated concretely: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a sha256 filter should show an Index Scan rather than a Seq Scan after normalizing, and firing two concurrent updates at two different chunks of the same file should show neither update lost.
